articles.title: More lawmakers report suspicious packages at offices
articles.summary: Several lawmakers said Friday their offices across the country had received suspicious mailings following reports earlier this week of letters containing unknown substances at U.S. election offices. Sens. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), Mike Rounds (R-S.D.), Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.), Tina Smith (D-Minn.) and over 15 House lawmakers said their district or state offices received these packages. Klobuchar…
articles.body:
Several lawmakers said Friday their offices across the country had received suspicious mailings following reports earlier this week of letters containing unknown substances at U.S. election offices.

Sens. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), Mike Rounds (R-S.D.), Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.), Tina Smith (D-Minn.) and over 15 House lawmakers said their district or state offices received these packages.

Klobuchar said in a Friday social media statement that officials intercepted the letter before it reached her Minnesota office.

“Thanks to the postal workers and investigators who identified and intercepted it, no one in our office was in immediate danger,” the Democratic senator wrote. “We’re grateful to everyone involved for their quick response and we will continue working closely with law enforcement as the investigation continues.”

Rounds shared an image of a letter sent to his Sioux Falls, N.D., office, and said the regional team contacted local authorities, who investigated and evacuated the office.

“This situation is deeply concerning and follows a trend of intimidating tactics that impact our team members,” he wrote on social media . “This has no place in our nation. America is better than this.”

California Reps. Laura Friedman (D), Jimmy Panetta (D), Gil Cisneros (D) and Linda Sánchez (D) all reported receiving suspicious packages at their district offices and said their staff members were safe.

Panetta, who represents the state’s 19th District, said a staff member at his Santa Cruz office opened an envelope that contained a “suspicious white powder.”

“Upon realizing that there was powder in the envelope, she immediately put the envelope in the garbage can, cleared fellow staff members out of the office, and called 911,” the lawmaker said in a social media post . “My priority is the safety and security of my staff and, thankfully, she and the other staff have been initially cleared by medical officials.”

In Florida, Democratic Reps. Maxwell Frost and Darren Soto shared similar reports from their district offices in Orlando and Kissimmee, respectively.

Soto shared on social media that his district office received “advance notice” from Frost’s Orlando office to “monitor our mail.”

“We are working with federal, state, and local law enforcement to support an investigation,” Soto continued. “Political violence has no place in our democracy, and we hope those who perpetrated this crime are brought to justice.”

On Thursday, spokespeople for two Democratic lawmakers, Sens. Chris Murphy (Conn.) and Alex Padilla (Calif.) told The Hill’s broadcast partner, NewsNation, they were notified that authorities intercepted suspicious packages addressed to their offices.

These suspicious mailings come just weeks ahead of the midterm elections . Before the 2024 presidential election, election officials in several states reported receiving packages that contained white powder.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.), whose district office also reported a similar package, decried the timing of these suspicious mailings in a statement shared on social media.

“This seemingly deliberate and widespread attack on our democracy and elections is unacceptable,” the Washington lawmaker wrote.

An FBI spokesperson told The Hill on Thursday that the agency was broadly inspecting reports of suspicious packages but declined to comment on specific instances.

“We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters,” the spokesperson said Thursday. “This FBI will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens.”

The Hill has reached out to the FBI and U.S. Capitol Police regarding these new reports.

articles.title: Trump puts new Russia sanctions that he recently signed into law on hold, citing national interest
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order that puts on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order that puts on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause was in the national interest.

Trump personally signed the legislation just last month and his move came just two days before a deadline set in the law itself for its implementation. It drew shift condemnation from congressional Democrats.

Named after late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham , the legislation had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling the war against Ukraine .

Trump's unexpected decision comes a week after he stunningly said the U.S. had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia.

An AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll published Oct. 1 found that Americans disapprove of the president's handling of the Iran war and blame him for higher prices. Trump's approval ratings have sunk to near-historic lows and pressure is mounting as Republicans try to hold control of both chambers of Congress after midterm elections on Nov. 3.

Sanctions were seen as part of Graham's legacy

Graham, a close ally and friend of the president, had just returned from Ukraine when he unexpectedly died in July. He had advocated for stricter U.S. sanctions against Russia as a way of pressuring it to end its war in Ukraine.

His colleagues in Congress responded with bipartisan support after his death and Trump attached his signature to the legislation — then changed his mind Friday.

The package had been meant to starve Russian President Vladimir Putin of the resources Moscow needs to continue its war in Ukraine after invading its neighbor more than four years ago. The bill, also drafted by Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., had sought to sanction Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving.

It also directed Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.

Blumenthal said in a statement that Trump was turning his back on "the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, and our European allies."

"These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin," Blumenthal said.

Democratic Virginia Rep. Don Beyer noted on social media shortly after the announcement of the sanctions being suspended that he and others had "warned" Trump might make such a move. The veteran congressman, who spoke out against the bill as it was debated, called on Congress to "fix this flawed law to stop Trump from capitulating to Putin and ensure that it truly supports Ukraine."

The White House did not immediately explain how pausing the sanctions was in the national interest. The decision was posted on the White House website late in the evening, and the notification noted that the report explaining the decision had been submitted to Congress.

Still, it comes as Trump has increasingly lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy , blaming him for failing to make a deal with Putin to end the fighting.

The Trump administration, meanwhile, had remained mostly quiet since the passage of the bill with large majorities in the House and Senate following Graham's sudden death — with lawmakers urged ahead by Zelenskyy.

Trump's action follows announced diesel deal with Putin

Under last week's agreement, Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."

Trump's striking a diesel deal with Putin has been pilloried by Republicans and Democrats alike who say it will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine -- without making a different to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump's war on Iran.

The sanctions that Trump has now suspended, meanwhile, also had become a campaign centerpiece for Sen. Darline Graham , the late senator's sister who was appointed to serve out the remaining months in his current term. She is now running to replace him in the Senate more permanently.

Darline Graham said in a statement after Trump signed the bill, "I wish Lindsey were here to celebrate this historic day." In a debate earlier this week with Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, Graham — who has Trump's endorsement and is expected to campaign with him in South Carolina next week — said she had been "so proud" to help get the measure passed.

She acknowledged, however, that it was the president's purview as to how he implemented it.

"It gives the president tools that he can use if he so chooses, to end the war through economic sanctions," Graham said Sunday during a debate in Columbia. "So that's up to him as to whether or not he wants to use it, or whether he wants to use something else, but I think the purpose of it is to bring down the gas prices and ultimately end the war. And when the war ends, gas prices will fall."

articles.title: Federal agents searched Omar’s trash for DNA before raid: Sources
articles.summary: Investigators have used secretive “dumpster diving” to obtain DNA when search warrants were not possible.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Federal agents collected garbage in hopes of obtaining the DNA of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) and her family before this week’s raid at her Washington, D.C. home, sources told NewsNation.

Investigators historically have used secretive “dumpster diving” to obtain DNA when search warrants were not possible or would have tipped off investigatory targets. It is legally permissible for law enforcement to collect trash that has been discarded for pickup and comb through it for genetic material.

Multiple sources familiar with the probe tell NewsNation that potential DNA evidence is critical to the investigation into Omar. They say the case is broader than the public may assume based on longstanding accusations surrounding her immigration history or marital status.

The investigation encompasses family members of the congresswoman, with evidence expected to go before a grand jury, sources said. Relatives of the lawmaker have been named in some of the subpoenas issued by federal prosecutors, NewsNation reported.

Federal agents seized Omar’s phone during a widely publicized search Monday at her Washington residence. NewsNation has learned that more than a dozen raids actually occurred simultaneously.

The case is being coordinated within the Minneapolis office of Homeland Security Investigations, suggesting it may be related to public benefits fraud committed by some members of the Somali immigrant community in the region.

The 44-year-old Omar, who seeks a fifth term in Congress, was born in Somalia and immigrated to the U.S. as a child in 1995. She was naturalized in 2000.

She originally was investigated by the Department of Justice under former President Biden before the case was closed. Parts of that investigation were reopened and expanded under the administration of President Trump.

Omar, a frequent political foil for Trump, said she believes the DOJ has been weaponized against her. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told Real America’s Voice Friday its case into the lawmaker is “about enforcing our nation’s laws.”

articles.title: Secret Service deputy chief stepping down
articles.summary: Matt Quinn, the deputy director of the U.S. Secret Service (USSS), announced Friday he was stepping down after a year-and-a-half in the role. Quinn said in a statement posted to social platform X he has been working with Secret Service Director Sean Curran on a transition plan for his role “for months now.” The deputy…
articles.body:
Matt Quinn, the deputy director of the U.S. Secret Service (USSS), announced Friday he was stepping down after a year-and-a-half in the role.

Quinn said in a statement posted to social platform X he has been working with Secret Service Director Sean Curran on a transition plan for his role “for months now.”

The deputy chief told NewsNation , The Hill’s broadcast partner, he is resigning from the post to spend more time with his family. His last day will be Nov. 7.

In a letter sent to Secret Service staff Friday obtained by NewsNation , Quinn called his 18 months in the role “the most rewarding of my career” and said stepping down was “not an easy decision.”

Quinn became the USSS’s deputy director after previously retiring from the agency following over two decades of work with them. He said in his departure note to staff that returning to the service had never been a long-term plan and that he informed Curran that “one of my goals was to work myself out of this job as quickly as possible.”

The deputy chief expressed confidence the agency is “well-positioned for the future.”

“The Secret Service has a long history of promoting from within, and I strongly believe that legacy is a positive one for the organization,” he wrote in his letter. “I wanted to help ensure that the Secret Service would never feel the need to look outside the organization to fill the Deputy Director role again. I know we have accomplished that goal.”

It is not yet clear who will replace Quinn in this role. The Hill has reached out to the Secret Service for comment.

In a joint “ 60 Minutes ” interview with Curran released earlier this week, Quinn addressed the rising number of threats the USSS has investigated this year. In July, the service’s director said it had opened over 10,000 investigations into threats made against its protectees — around a 40 percent increase from that time last year.

“I think the biggest factor we’re dealing with today is mental health issues for sure,” Quinn told CBS News’s Norah O’Donnell when asked specifically about threats made against President Trump. “And more people are being pushed over the edge in either direction.”

Quinn’s departure coincides with several high-profile departures within the Trump administration this week.

On Friday, the White House announced its newly appointed press secretary, Katie Zacharia, would leave her post after only five days amid scrutiny over her legal qualifications and preparedness for the position. Former U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle similarly resigned Tuesday after Trump requested she step down following criticism over her relationship with a GOP donor.

articles.title: California officials who process ballots from suspected noncitizens risk prosecution, U.S. warns
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — The Trump administration is escalating its fight with California ahead of next month’s midterm election, warning that local officials who process and tabulate ballots submitted by suspected noncitizen voters are putting themselves at risk of criminal investigation and potential prosecution.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Trump administration is escalating its fight with California ahead of next month’s midterm election, warning that local officials who process and tabulate ballots submitted by suspected noncitizen voters are putting themselves at risk of criminal investigation and potential prosecution. The letter Friday from a senior Justice Department official and obtained first by The Associated Press is the latest salvo in an ongoing tussle with heavily Democratic California, coming just a day after the Trump administration sued the state to prevent it from counting mail ballots from people the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed. “The legal consequences for either facilitating or ignoring a federal crime are significant. Noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime — and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful,” warns the letter from Trent McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general at the Justice Department. It adds: “If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime.” The letter is addressed to the Los Angeles County Counsel’s office and also is copied to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan, effectively putting the entire state on notice. In response to the letter, Logan said his office is focused on conducting a fair and secure election while noting that Election Day is a mere 18 days away. “The U.S. Department of Justice has chosen to litigate their unverified assertions of voting eligibility. At this point, it is best for this to be addressed in court,” he said. The other offices and the state attorney general did not immediately respond to requests for comment. It is unclear how many individuals the Justice Department might look to try to investigate and charge, though any federal criminal cases in the Los Angeles area would be handled by the office of Bill Essayli, the region’s top federal prosecutor and one of the Justice Department officials who filed the federal complaint Thursday against California. Trump weighed in late Friday, sharing on Truth Social a link to a news story about the letter and adding: “They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!” The Trump administration has made the pursuit of noncitizen voters a priority Sent less than three weeks before the Nov. 3 election, the letter adds to simmering tensions over voter rolls between California and the Justice Department and reflects the Trump administration’s aggressive hunt for noncitizen voters. It has made the issue a priority this year, including by demanding detailed voter information — including dates of birth, addresses, driver’s license numbers and partial Social Security numbers — from the states. The Justice Department has charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election. In July, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin sent letters to California, Nevada, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, alleging that as many as 250,000 noncitizens were registered in those states. Election officials there were skeptical of the claim, including Weber, the California secretary of state. That same month, the Republican administration claimed Nevada had 1,500 noncitizen voters on its voter rolls. But after the federal government identified them to the state, the number of actual registered noncitizens turned out to be zero. That experience is backed up by research and investigations in various states, which make clear that voting by noncitizens is extremely rare. The letter follows a Justice Department lawsuit The Justice Department lawsuit was filed after California officials were given, and did not meet, a 48-hour deadline to review a password-protected thumb drive that contained a list of 20,000 names. The federal government says those are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election, although the secretary of state said the administration has provided no evidence to support that claim. The state mails ballots to all registered voters. Rick Hasen, a UCLA law professor, said the letter “ups the ante by threatening election officials with potential criminal prosecution.” “It is deplorable that rather than work cooperatively and assist states in their election administration responsibilities, the federal government is making escalating threats and unreasonable demands beyond its power in the middle of an ongoing election,” he said. Justin Levitt, a former deputy assistant attorney general who teaches at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles, dismissed the idea that an attempted prosecution of an election official using the letter’s rationale would hold up. “Courts haven’t been buying what DOJ has been selling, and nothing in this letter is calibrated to change course,” he said. “Fortunately, election officials — not just in Los Angeles, but across the country — are equipped to stand up to aggressive bullying. And the law is on their side.” Over 23 million people are registered statewide, and a handful of competitive congressional races in other California districts could determine which party controls the U.S. House for the final two years of President Donald Trump’s term. The Trump administration’s escalating threats against California come as Democratic lawmakers are urging the Justice Department to honor its longstanding policy of not interfering in U.S. elections. Earlier Friday, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., and Dick Durbin, D-Ill., wrote to Attorney General Todd Blanche demanding that the Justice Department commit to not seizing ballots or other election materials before the midterm elections are certified.

articles.title: Zacharia speaks out after White House press secretary exit: ‘It was an honor’
articles.summary: Katie Zacharia issued her first public statement Friday night after a White House official announced she’d be “transitioning out” of the press secretary post after just five days in the role. In a post on the social media platform X, Zacharia praised President Trump’s leadership, saying, “It was an honor to work for him.” “President…
articles.body:
Katie Zacharia issued her first public statement Friday night after a White House official announced she’d be “transitioning out” of the press secretary post after just five days in the role.

In a post on the social media platform X , Zacharia praised President Trump’s leadership, saying, “It was an honor to work for him.”

“President Trump is a kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man,” she wrote in her post, which included a picture of herself and Trump in the Oval Office.

She continued, “I wish more Americans appreciated him. No one will ever make America great the way he has and continues to.”

Zacharia’s departure follows the president’s remarks to reporters on Friday that he had advised her to “reconsider” the position. The former political commentator has now logged the shortest press secretary tenure in the position’s history.

Her exit also followed a wave of scrutiny over a shaky debut press conference , which lasted 14 minutes and included only three questions from conservative-leaning outlets, as well as skepticism over her legal background.

Zacharia, who replaced former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, had presented herself as a lawyer during her TV appearances. When asked by a reporter on Tuesday about which state she passed the bar exam in, Zacharia responded, “When I moved to China.”

However, the Wall Street Journal reported later that evening that she had failed the exam , prompting watchdog group Campaign for Accountability to file a complaint with the State Bar of California on Wednesday over her claims that she is a lawyer.

In an interview with conservative outlet Real America’s Voice, Zacharia said she “misheard” the question but added that her bar exam results were “inconsequential” because she moved to China with her husband for work after graduation.

Anthony Scaramucci, who served as White House communications director during Trump’s first term for 11 days, responded to Zacharia’s departure on Friday.

“Records are made to be broken,” Scaramucci wrote on social media . “But I take no pleasure in other people’s pain.”

Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., just last month. The bill took aim at Russia’s largest buyers of oil and gas, allowing the president to impose tariffs on goods from those countries, which may include China and India. Passed with bipartisan support, the bill was intended to target Russia’s revenue streams as the country continues to wage its war against Ukraine. Suspending the sanctions provides Russia a financial lifeline. Trump’s decision to put a hold on the sanctions package comes after he announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin last week to release hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel fuel onto the global market as fuel prices soar. Trump has expressed frustration with Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil and gas infrastructure and has blamed them for the increase in fuel costs while downplaying the impact of the Iran war on the oil market. The decision to waive the Russia sanctions drew swift condemnation from critics in Congress. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., called the move a “craven, cowardly action” in a statement. “These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin,” Blumenthal said. Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., a staunch Ukraine ally, said “the president is prolonging the war, not ending it,” in a post on X. Trump’s move to pause the sanctions comes as the price of diesel fuel has shot up almost 70% since the war in Iran began in February and comes less than three weeks before the midterm elections, as cost of living remains a top issue for voters. Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., who co-sponsored the bill named for her late brother, has touted its success as a key part of her campaign to win a full term in his Senate seat. Graham is a fierce Trump ally, as his endorsement was critical in her GOP primary win. Graham has yet to criticize the president for his Russian oil deal or the decision to halt the sanctions. Congress passed the legislation with strong majorities in both the House and Senate, though many Democrats opposed the bill because it granted the president new tariff powers. The legislation states that before the administration waives the new sanctions, it must submit an unclassified report to Congress explaining its basis. In his executive order, Trump said the White House has sent the report to Capitol Hill.

articles.title: Trump puts on hold new Russia sanctions he signed into law
articles.summary: US president’s executive order comes two days before sanctions deadline and a week after diesel deal with Putin.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has put on hold a sweeping package of sanctions on Russia that he signed into law last month, telling Congress the pause is in the national interest.

Trump signed an executive order on Friday, two days before a deadline in the law that would put the sanctions into effect.

The law – named after Lindsey Graham, the Republican senator who died unexpectedly in July after returning from Ukraine – had passed in the House of Representatives and the Senate by large margins. The bipartisan legislation was drafted by Graham and Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal.

It sought to starve Moscow of money for the war by sanctioning Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers carrying its energy.

It also directed Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on the five biggest importers of Russian oil or gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15 percent of Russia’s natural gas exports and are taking steps to cut them.

The decision to suspend the sanctions comes a week after Trump said the US had signed a deal to buy diesel from Russia to try to lower global fuel prices.

Both Republicans and Democrats, criticising the deal , said it would help Russia’s war effort without affecting fuel prices.

Democratic Representative Don Beyer said he and others had “warned” that Trump might do this, in reference to Trump’s deal with Moscow.

Beyer called on Congress to “fix this flawed law to stop Trump from capitulating to Putin and ensure that it truly supports Ukraine”.

Trump has also increasingly criticised Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy lately for failing to reach a deal with Russia.

As Republicans try to keep control of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections, an AP-NORC poll released on October 1 found Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of the Iran war and blame him for higher prices among several other domestic policy issues.

"No creo que Katie deba sufrir como está sufriendo a manos de la prensa", ha indicado. "Le dije que creo que es mejor que sea feliz. No estoy seguro de que puedas ser feliz en este trabajo. No hay nada fácil en este trabajo", ha manifestado. Es más, Trump iba más allá para justificar esta decisión tomada. "Nos gusta mucho, ha hecho una labor fantástica... Katie ha sido tratada muy mal por los medios. Muy, muy mal. Muy injusto. Le pregunté: '¿Esto es para ti?'. Y es una buena persona. Voy a dejar que ella tome esa decisión. Sean Hannity fue un poco duro. Katie ha empezado mal, las noticias han sido muy desagradables con ella. Le dije, 'Sinceramente, si yo fuera tú, lo reconsideraría". "Es un gran honor para mí haber nombrado recientemente a Katie Zacharia como secretaria de prensa", había escrito el mandatario en su red Truth Social. "Tiene un historial de apoyo intachable y ha sido una seguidora leal y brillante desde el principio. ¡Además, es una fanática devota y miembro de MAGA (Make America Great Again, "Hagamos a EE.UU. grande nuevamente")!", añadió. Lo que sucede es que la presión del cargo se la ha llevado por delante. Protagonizó un accidentado estreno en la Casa Blanca al confundir las palabras “presidente” y “marido” durante su primera comparecencia. Casada con el productor de Hollywood Tyler Zacharia y madre de cuatro hijos, la portavoz cuenta con una trayectoria vinculada al conservadurismo estadounidense. Estudió Humanidades y Derecho en la Universidad de Pepperdine, presidió una agrupación de Jóvenes Republicanos y realizó prácticas en la Casa Blanca durante la presidencia de George W. Bush. si bien no ejerció como abogada.

articles.title: The Memo: Ukraine’s slide into crisis sharpens questions for Trump
articles.summary: Tumult and doubt are hanging over the role of the United States in the war in Ukraine, 4 1/2 years after the Russian invasion. articles.body:
Tumult and doubt are hanging over the role of the United States in the war in Ukraine, 4 1/2 years after the Russian invasion.

That’s the bottom line after a week of high drama that roiled Washington, Kyiv and concerned political leaders in Europe.

The U.S. stance is, of course, determined by President Trump, often in unpredictable fashion.

On Friday, he denied to reporters that either he or his sometime ally Elon Musk had decided to restrict Ukrainian usage of the Starshield satellite system, which is vital to the effectiveness of Kyiv’s drones.

“I didn’t do that. No, we didn’t do that at all. In fact, I don’t even think it was slowed down from what I understood. Because I just checked this morning,” Trump told reporters Friday as he left the White House en route to a campaign rally in Georgia.

The Ukrainians are adamant that the system was indeed slowed down — one of several developments about which they are incensed, blaming the U.S. for having undermined a war effort that they have fought against the odds and at enormous cost.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told a Friday news conference in Brussels that the initial slowing down of the Starshield system had come as “a dangerous and unpleasant surprise,” according to The Associated Press .

Zelensky also disputed the idea that the system had been restored to normal function.

“Have they returned to previous speed limits? No. But is it coming back? Yes,” he said.

The Starshield issue was perhaps the most shocking episode in a recent chapter of drama and recrimination between Kyiv and the White House.

Trump’s Oct. 9 announcement of a deal for Russian diesel caused widespread consternation, given its capacity to ease economic pressure on Moscow. Zelensky and his allies had been seeking to ramp up this pressure. In Washington, Congress recently passed legislation , in memory of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), intensifying sanctions against Moscow.

Trump’s assertion that there was an “Energy Ceasefire” between the warring parties has come to seem hollow.

Russia never appeared to accede to the idea of a mutual pause on hitting infrastructure facilities, and Ukraine duly abandoned its willingness to hold off striking Russian refineries.

There have also been conflicting reports about whether the United States was withholding intelligence from Ukraine, which Trump has denied.

Recent days have been interspersed with heated words.

Trump has suggested Ukraine should replace Zelensky as its president. In an interview with Newsmax, broadcast Thursday evening, Trump complained that Zelensky is “not a good guy for us to deal with” and also appeared to blame the Ukrainian president, at least in part, for having “destroyed that country.”

Zelensky, for his part, this week told British journalist Piers Morgan that he felt his nation had been betrayed, in part by the diesel deal. He also told Morgan that he regretted that Ukraine was “losing” the U.S. as a strong partner.

Amid all the bleakness, it looks as if U.S.-Ukraine relations are at their lowest ebb since the infamous February 2025 Oval Office meeting at which Zelensky was berated by Trump and Vice President Vance.

The effects on the battlefield are plain to see.

According to the AP, the latest spate of Russian attacks hit at least nine areas of Ukraine, leaving “hundreds of thousands of households” without power. Those attacks will bite with special fierceness as winter sets in across eastern Europe.

Trump, pinioned by rising gas prices stemming from the war on Iran that he launched in conjunction with Israel earlier this year, appears to be trying to shift blame to Ukraine for pain at American pumps.

His social media message announcing the diesel deal said that the new arrangement — as well as what he inaccurately termed American “TOTAL CONTROL” of the Strait of Hormuz — would mean that “Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!”

According to AAA , the average U.S. diesel price Friday was approximately $6.33, up from $6.28 on the day Trump announced the Russia deal — and hugely increased from the $3.65 level at which it stood one year ago.

Rick Tyler, a Republican strategist who is often critical of Trump, complained that the diesel deal amounted to “amateur hour.”

“It won’t work, and yet people are going to think we are going to get lower gas prices,” Tyler told this column.

He also blasted Trump’s general approach as “despicable” and said, regarding the president’s approach to Russian President Vladimir Putin, that Trump was “sacrificing the credibility of the United States when he engages with a thug like that who is killing innocent civilians.”

Meanwhile, confusion and controversy continue to swirl around the specifics of the Starlink matter.

On Thursday evening, Reuters reported that the order to limit the way the system could be used by Ukraine “came from inside the White House.” The news agency sourced that information to “two U.S. officials and a Western official.”

In addition to Trump’s Friday denial that either he or Musk was responsible, a U.S. official also told NewsNation, “No such request was ever made by the President.” (NewsNation and The Hill are both owned by Nexstar Media Group.)

Then, late Friday, The Telegraph reported that it was Musk who had “approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine.” Musk had previously implicitly denied he played any decisive role.

Meanwhile in Washington, four GOP senators joined with Democratic colleagues in seeking more information about the Pentagon’s role in the episode.

Whatever more is revealed about the specifics, there’s no mistaking the consternation felt by Republicans outside of Trump’s most fervent MAGA base about the current situation.

Doug Heye, a former communications director for the Republican National Committee, contrasted Trump, very unfavorably, with the vigorous opposition to Moscow evinced by former President Reagan in the 1980s.

“It’s another 180, and it’s very depressing for anyone who considers themselves a traditional Republican,” Heye said.

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: Trump administration says painting Eisenhower building would hurt landmark’s history
articles.summary: The Trump administration’s plan to put a coat of white paint on the exterior of the Eisenhower Executive Office Building would diminish the historic character of the 19th-century landmark, according to a draft environmental assessment published Friday. “The unpainted exterior granite walls, including their natural detail (e.g., grey and pink hues), were hand-selected by the…
articles.body:
The Trump administration’s plan to put a coat of white paint on the exterior of the Eisenhower Executive Office Building would diminish the historic character of the 19 th -century landmark, according to a draft environmental assessment published Friday .

“The unpainted exterior granite walls, including their natural detail (e.g., grey and pink hues), were hand-selected by the architect and are central to the building’s historic character and original design intent,” the assessment read.

The administration’s proposal to paint the Eisenhower building is a part of President Trump’s larger plan of beautifying the nation’s capital. The exterior paint job is estimated to cost at least $7.5 billion.

The proposal alarmed preservationists, architects, historians and others who argue that granite is not meant to be painted and that paint would trap moisture and deteriorate the stone.

Friday’s report found that the proposed white mineral silica paint is weather resistant and permeable enough that it is unlikely for moisture to be trapped beneath the surface, according to the assessment report.

“Mineral silicate paints are advertised as highly breathable and durable wall coatings that are composed of natural minerals and potassium silicate,” the report noted.

In August, a federal judge allowed the administration to conduct paint tests on the 19th-century building after finding that concerns raised by preservation groups did not prove the testing could cause “irreparable harm.” The judge said the ruling applied only to testing and not the entire project.

Trump has previously criticized the building’s appearance, saying last year that its gray exterior is a “really bad color.”

The Eisenhower building sits next door to the White House and was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1969. It was also listed on the National Register of Historic Places and the District of Columbia Inventory of Historic Sites in 1972.
